structure.title: Message from the Chairman
structure.summary: The Chairman's message reviews FY 2024-25 as a transformative year for IndusInd Bank amid global geopolitical shifts, trade tensions, and slowing domestic growth. It acknowledges internal governance lapses and outlines board-led reforms emphasizing ethics, compliance, and sustainability. Global economic challenges include US tariff measures and reduced IMF forecasts, while India's GDP growth slowed to 6.5% with coordinated fiscal-monetary stimulus. The bank faced asset quality pressures but maintains a robust balance sheet. Business highlights cover digital initiatives, leadership transition with new MD & CEO Rajiv Anand, strategic focus areas, ESG efforts with 47% sustainable finance portfolio, and operational resilience during Operation Sindoor. The Chairman thanks stakeholders and employees.

nodes.title: Message from the Chairman (intro)
nodes.summary: The Chairman's message to shareholders reviews the 2024-25 financial year as a watershed for IndusInd Bank, set against a complex global environment with geopolitical shifts, slowing domestic and banking growth, and easing monetary policy. It acknowledges internal challenges that prompted swift, transparent board actions, catalyzing a transformation rooted in ethics, accountability, transparency, and sustainability. The Board and Management conducted a rigorous review and implemented structural reforms to reinforce integrity, compliance, and high governance standards. The Chairman thanks stakeholders for their support. Additionally, the message notes India's GDP growth slowed to 6.5% after three years averaging 8.8%, with investment moderating due to slower government capex from underutilized budgets.

nodes.title: Global Economic Horizon
nodes.summary: The text covers global elections in FY 2024-25, including India's re-election of the NDA government, which supported economic stability. It highlights the US election of President Trump and subsequent trade-restrictive measures with high tariffs, causing uncertainty that dampens investment and tightens financial conditions. The IMF reduced global growth forecasts for 2025 and 2026 by 0.3%, with significant downward revisions for the US and China in 2026. Protracted geopolitical and US trade tariff tensions pose serious risks, with potential cascading impacts on India's growth outlook.

nodes.title: Domestic Economic Developments and Outlook
nodes.summary: The text covers India's economic developments: GDP growth slowed to 6.5% after averaging 8.8% over three years, with moderated investment due to government capex underutilization, recovering private consumption, and positive net external demand from service exports. Supply-side: strong farm growth, resilient services, but manufacturing decelerated. Banking sector credit growth moderated to 12% (March 2025) from 16.3%, dipping below 10% in Q1 FY2026. Coordinated fiscal and monetary stimulus included RBI rate cuts (25 bps in Feb/Apr, 50 bps in June) and liquidity infusion via CRR cuts and durable instruments totaling ₹8 trillion, with a possible 100 bps CRR cut in H2 FY2025. FY2026 Union Budget balanced fiscal discipline with capex push and tax relief targeting agriculture, MSMEs, investment, and exports. Forex reserves rose despite capital outflows. GDP growth is projected at 6-6.5%, with domestic orientation and trade negotiations limiting tariff impact. Spillovers from global shocks may be countered by monetary easing and forex buffers; macro-financial stability supports growth. Additionally, IndusInd Bank's FY2025 faced challenges including slower industry growth, asset quality pressures in unsecured segments, and material governance/accounting lapses, prompting a transformation focused on ethics, compliance, and sustainability. The Board and Management addressed issues with higher governance standards; the balance sheet remains robust with healthy capital adequacy, provision coverage, and liquidity.

structure.title: 1. Macroeconomic and Banking Environment
structure.summary: The text covers the macroeconomic and banking environment for FY2024-25, highlighting global political shifts, including India's policy continuity and US trade tensions. It details India's GDP growth easing to 6.5%, with resilient activity, moderating investment, and strong services exports. Monetary policy easing is described, with repo rate cuts and liquidity infusion to support growth amid easing inflation. Fiscal policy focuses on discipline, capex, and tax relief. Banking sector credit growth moderated but remained healthy, with improved asset quality. External sector fundamentals strengthened with higher forex reserves and a low current account deficit, despite rupee depreciation.

structure.summary: The text covers the business overview and operating performance of a bank for FY2025, including financial results such as interest earned, net interest income, operating profit, net profit, and balance sheet parameters like deposits, advances, and balance sheet size. It discusses the global economic challenges and India's growth outlook, and details the bank's strategic responses: deposit retailization, calibrated loan growth with reductions in unsecured and corporate lending, asset quality stress in microfinance, digital banking initiatives (INDIE app), governance improvements following control gaps, and overall financial outcomes with capital adequacy and liquidity buffers.

structure.title: 3. Consumer Banking
structure.summary: The text covers Consumer Banking, including consumer liabilities with strategic initiatives for deposit mobilization, customer-centric innovation, new customer acquisitions, cross-selling, omnichannel strategy, and segment-specific offerings like Indus Grande Care, Indus Care, and Indus Privilege Prime. It also details SME and Merchant Acquiring, highlighting the Consumer Current Account portfolio, Indus One Business product, digital onboarding, merchant acquiring traction, and the upcoming INDIE for Business platform. Retail Payments growth is driven by UPI transaction volumes. Client Wealth Management covers Bancassurance and investment services with open architecture and expanded product lines. RACC – Retail Assets and Cards encompasses retail agriculture (loans to farmers, insurance, government schemes), Loan Against Property, Prime Home Loans, Personal Loans, Credit Cards (including new premium cards), and Business Banking Group (MSME focus, hub-and-spoke model, digital transformation, and initiatives like IndusWE and Vyapar Vaar).

structure.title: 4. Affluent Banking
structure.summary: The text covers IndusInd Bank's Affluent Banking under the PIONEER brand, detailing its growth metrics (19% NRV CAGR, 22% liabilities CAGR, 17% fee income CAGR, NRV over ₹1.2 lakh crore), Private Banking launch, and three-pronged strategy: client-first approach, deep distribution with relationship managers, and future-ready tech stack using AI/ML. It highlights PIONEER Private targeting top-tier clients. NRI Banking shows 28% growth in liabilities, 2.6x market share increase since 2019, expansion of remittance platform and FCY products, dedicated NRI branches, digital onboarding, and virtual service teams. The IBU at GIFT City details its $3.3 billion balance sheet, offshore services including deposits, loans, trade credits, derivatives, treasury products, global markets desk, 13.58% market share in customer liabilities, and advisory roles with IFSCA.

structure.title: 5. Consumer Finance Division
structure.summary: The text describes the Consumer Finance Division (CFD), which leads vehicle financing across commercial vehicles, auto loans, two-wheelers, tractors, and construction equipment for new and pre-owned assets, and supports affordable housing for financial inclusion. It reports FY2025 portfolio growth to 3 million loans and ₹97,898 crore outstanding (8% increase), with auto loans growing 15% and LCVs 13%. Disbursements totaled 9.89 lakh loans worth ₹47,614 crore, with stable auto, commercial vehicle, construction equipment, and two-wheeler segments, but declined tractor funding due to stricter underwriting. Operations are supported by a Chennai back office handling 50 million transactions, and mobile applications enable seamless approvals.

structure.title: 6. Bharat Financial Inclusion Limited
structure.summary: This section covers Bharat Financial Inclusion Limited (BFIL), an IndusInd Bank subsidiary providing microfinance and related services across 1.62 lakh villages. It reviews macroeconomic and rural indicators, including GDP growth, CPI easing, FMCG demand, tractor and two-wheeler sales, and rural credit and deposit growth. It discusses rising rural consumption and FY2025 microfinance sector pressures, including a 13.9% portfolio decline and delinquency trends. BFIL's performance is detailed: net portfolio ₹37,381 crore, 78 lakh borrowers, disbursements, women's empowerment, and operational challenges. Merchant loans through Bharat Super Shop (17 lakh merchants, ₹7,260 crore book) and liability accounts (191 lakh accounts, ₹2,680 crore deposits) are covered, along with the Bharat Money Store network (80,936 outlets, 50.3 lakh customers, ₹4,882 crore transactions). CSR initiatives—Bharat Sanjeevani livestock care, Bharat PRAGAT watershed and healthcare, and NRLM livestock programs—are summarized, plus new programs, egg sales, market linkages, SOPs, and alignment with 12 of 17 SDGs.

nodes.title: Rural Indicators
nodes.summary: The text covers Bharat Financial Inclusion Limited (BFIL), a wholly owned subsidiary of IndusInd Bank, detailing its role as a business correspondent providing microfinance loans, merchant financing, deposit products, and remittances to underserved communities, with a presence in over 1.62 lakh villages across 550+ districts in 23 states, supported by 32,000+ field staff. It then discusses the macro economy and sector outlook, noting India's real GDP growth of 6.5% in FY2025, GVA growth of 6.4%, and CPI easing to 3.34%. Rural indicators are highlighted, including FMCG volume growth of 7.1% in Q3 FY2025 with rural demand up 9.9%, tractor sales up 8.4% for FY2025, rural and semi-urban deposit growth of 9.5% and credit growth of 12.6%, and two-wheeler sales at 1.9 crore units, up 9.3%.

nodes.title: Consumer Spending, Microfinance Sector Trends, and BFIL Performance FY2025
nodes.summary: The page covers rising private consumption with rural household spending doubling and increased non-food expenditure, creating opportunities for BFIL's consumer durable, hospice cash, and rural mobility loans. It reviews the microfinance sector's FY2025 pressures—elevated borrower leverage, regional disruptions, tighter onboarding, and a 13.9% gross loan portfolio decline to ₹3.81 lakh crore, with rising later-stage delinquencies but improving early delinquencies; outlook for FY2026 growth and asset quality focus. It details BFIL's assets: net portfolio ₹37,381 crore (down 12.7%), active borrowers 78 lakh, branches 3,756, disbursements ₹44,305 crore (down 17.3%), serving 169 lakh clients. Microfinance business empowers women entrepreneurs through high-touch and technology models across 1.6 lakh villages, 468 districts, 21 states, serving 77 lakh women borrowers and 108 lakh depositors; FY2025 challenges included elections, loan waiver campaigns, heat waves, and Karnataka ordinance; loan book ₹29,960 crore with cautious disbursement, 21% H2 recovery, and improved collection efficiency.

nodes.title: Loans to Merchants
nodes.summary: BFIL provides credit and banking services to nano-entrepreneurs via Bharat Super Shop (BSS), covering zero-balance accounts, deposits, loans, and payments; as of March 2025, BSS operated in 558 cities, serving 17 lakh merchants with a ₹7,260 crore loan book. BFIL's liability book shows 191 lakh active accounts and ₹2,680 crore in deposits. structure.summary: The text discusses the Global Diamonds and Jewellery Group (GDJG), highlighting the Gems and Jewellery Industry's role in India's exports, employment, and MSME growth. In FY2025, corporate India grew moderately, and the Bank's corporate book stood at ₹1,43,463 crore, with a tactical reduction in H2 and focus on mid-corporates. Strategic priorities for FY2026 include deepening mid/small corporate leadership, enhancing client profitability, building a sustainable liability base, and maintaining underwriting excellence. The text details client coverage groups (Corporate & Institutional, Commercial, Emerging Local Corporate), specialized verticals (Real Estate, Financial Services, Education & Healthcare, Agriculture), Supply Chain Finance, marketing initiatives, Investment Banking, Public Sector Group, and Financial Institution Group.

structure.summary: The text details IndusInd Bank's digital transformation in FY2025 under its Digital 2.0 agenda, covering the strategic roadmap and growth of digital business, including customer acquisition, assets, and liabilities. It highlights the scale-up of the INDIE platform, launch of INDIE for Business for MSMEs, revamped net banking, and a new GIFT City app. It also covers the EasyCredit lending platform, digital marketing campaigns, digital partnerships, advanced analytics and machine learning models, and WhatsApp banking and chatbot initiatives, including performance metrics, features, and future plans.

structure.title: 10. Global Markets Group
structure.summary: The Global Markets Group (GMG) comprises Asset Liability Management (ALM), Trading across rates, equities, FX, derivatives, and commodities, and Client Sales including Financial Markets Sales & Solutions and Credit Sales. ALM ensures regulatory compliance (CRR, SLR, LCR, IDL, NSFR) and manages liquidity and funding strategies. Trading desks handle proprietary positions, market-making, and client liquidity. Credit Sales provides debt capital market solutions and placements. Financial Markets Sales offers customized hedging and bullion solutions, plus exchange-traded currency derivatives. GMG expanded offshore via GIFT City IBU and new products under IFSCA. The Bank maintains board-approved policies, real-time risk monitoring, BCP drills, and an Integrated Treasury Application for seamless transaction flow.

structure.title: 11. Transaction Banking Group
structure.summary: The Transaction Banking Group (TBG) offers Cash Management Services (CMS), Trade Services/Finance, and Global Remittance products via digital platforms. CMS includes customized payables/receivables, escrow, and API-based collections (NACH, BBPS, UPI) for segments like NBFCs and real estate, plus capital market escrow and PPI settlements. Government/PSU integration covers IFMS, GeM, PFMS, ICEGATE, and tax payments. QR smart address systems for municipal/panchayat disbursements are noted. Trade services cover large, medium, and MSME clients in India and GIFT City, including factoring, LC discounting, and export finance. The Bank is a major cross-border remittance player. Digital platforms support payments, payroll, tax, EPFO/ESIC, bank guarantees, LCs, remittances, and trade dashboards, with e-stamping, digital document execution, and electronic bank guarantees. Connected Banking with Tally ERP (Indus Direct) grew. The Bank is an IBDIC founding member and executed the first ITFS export factoring transaction via GIFT City.

structure.title: Client Management, Liabilities, and Financial Restructuring Groups Overview
key_items: 12. Client Management and Pan Bank Liabilities Group
structure.summary: Section 12 introduces the Client Management Group, including its Decision Sciences and Client Experience Units, which use analytics and omnichannel engagement to deepen client relationships. It outlines the Approach & Principles: proactive relationship management, data-driven client understanding, seamless omnichannel experience, and a data-driven culture. The group targets client activation, engagement, cross-sell, retention, and win-back to boost lifetime value. The Pan Bank Liabilities Group drives liability strategy, emphasizing granular retail and SBC deposits, which contributed ~59% of FY2025 deposit growth. Together they form a client-first ecosystem aligning engagement with sustainable liability growth. Section 13 covers the Financial Restructuring and Reconstruction Group, which handles NPA recovery, stressed asset restructuring, NPA sales, NCLT activities, and a dedicated NCLT desk, using SARFAESI, RDDB, and RBI tools such as the Prudential Framework.

structure.title: 14. General Banking Operations
structure.summary: The text covers general banking operations, including strengthened KYC policies with simplified procedures for lower-income groups and digital e-KYC via mobile app and video-based CIP. It highlights a workflow and imaging system for faster processing across account opening, term deposits, trade finance, and branch expenses. Clearing operations include CTS across 2,650 branches, NACH/ECS, and ABPS. The Bank has policies for deceased depositor claims, deposits, fair practice, citizens' charter, customer compensation, unclaimed deposits (with DEAF transfers), customer rights, and customer protection against unauthorized electronic transactions. It emphasizes customer centricity, non-discrimination, and accessibility for differently-abled and senior citizens through talking ATMs, braille, ramps, and doorstep banking.

structure.summary: The text details Corporate and Global Markets Operations (CGMO) at IndusInd Bank, covering its comprehensive services including trade, supply chain finance, remittances, cash management, forex, derivatives, bullion, and depository services, with a focus on digital transformation, efficiency, and talent development. It highlights customer-centric initiatives such as cash/cheque pickup optimization, a Trade Digital Servicing team, RPA-automated outward remittances, and processing 534 IPOs, leading to improved NPS. People initiatives include capability building, Skill Quest, and recognition programs. Capability enhancements involve CMS platform upgrades, digitized bank guarantee workflows via iTrac, and RPA integration with SWIFT/SFMS. Risk management uses RCSA and KRIs. structure.title: 16. Branch Network and Infrastructure
structure.summary: The Bank's nationwide network includes 3,081 banking outlets and 3,027 ATMs across all 28 states and six of eight union territories. It has an International Banking Unit at GIFT City and representative offices in London, Dubai, and Abu Dhabi. Fifteen PIONEER branches are located in major cities such as Mumbai, Pune, Delhi, Gurugram, Chandigarh, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Jaipur, Ahmedabad, and Noida. Six currency chests are operated in Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, and Chandigarh.

structure.title: 17. Information Technology
structure.summary: The Information Technology section covers IndusInd Bank's FY2025 technology modernization, digital transformation, and infrastructure operations. Key points include: end-to-end digital transformation and innovative products for operational efficiency; strategic investments in a secure Core Banking platform and channel applications; transformation of the legacy data warehouse into a public cloud-hosted Enterprise Data Platform with Data Lakehouse architecture optimized for Generative AI; and significant cybersecurity enhancements (micro-segmentation, IAM, EDR, SIEM, firewalls, IDS/IPS, MFA). It details modernization of Core Banking (Finacle high availability, 200-300% batch improvement) and the UPI platform (cloud-hosted, containerized, 99.999% uptime, 400ms transactions, near-zero RPO). A new Wealth Management platform is launched. Data platforms include the Enterprise Data Platform (medallion architecture, near-real-time ingestion, ~100 source systems, 1.5PB data) and a microfinance Data Lakehouse for BFIL. GenAI adoption for DevSecOps with MS Co-Pilot is noted. Infrastructure modernization covers O365 staff productivity and SD-WAN network. UI/UX innovations include GIFT City mobile banking, IndusNet revamp, and INDIE Digital Banking for MSME. Technology awards (Infosys Finacle, IBS Intelligence, Finnoviti) are listed.

structure.title: 18. Human Resources
structure.summary: IndusInd Bank was certified as a 'Great Place to Work' for the third consecutive year, reflecting its commitment to credibility, respect, fairness, pride, transparency, and camaraderie. The HR agenda focuses on succession planning, talent development, engagement, retention, digitization, welfare, and wellness. As of March 31, 2025, the workforce was 44,974, supported by diversified hiring channels including referrals, job portals, consultants, campuses, social media, and a 'Hire-Train-Deploy' model. The Bank emphasizes robust succession planning, continuous learning and development with over 16 lakh learning man-hours and the 'Indus Evolve' app, performance management aligned with KRAs and SMART objectives, and a 'Pay for Performance' compensation philosophy with ESOPs. Employee engagement initiatives include quarterly webcasts, 'We Connect,' 'Coffee Connect,' 'Appreciation Day,' festivals, sports events, service awards, and the Life Event Assistance Program. Welfare benefits include paternity leave, career guidance, volunteering leave, women empowerment policies, and an Employee Welfare Fund. Digitization efforts feature digital onboarding, a chatbot, online staff accounts, a career platform, a learning management system, and mobile apps. The Bank ensures compliance with regulatory norms and promotes its Code of Conduct.

structure.title: 19. Employees Stock Option Scheme
structure.summary: The text outlines the IndusInd Bank Employee Stock Option Scheme 2020 (ESOS 2020), approved on September 25, 2020, which replaced the ESOS 2007. ESOS 2020 allows the Board and Compensation Committee to grant options up to 7% of paid-up equity shares, per SEBI guidelines. Vesting occurs at specified times with a minimum one-year period between grant and vesting; unvested options expire as stipulated or within five years. Exercise price is set by the Compensation Committee, typically based on the latest closing price and not below face value. Vested options must be exercised within five years. Options are equity-settled, with one share per option. Additionally, the IBL Special Incentive ESOS for BFIL Merger 2018 (ESOS 2018), approved on December 11, 2018, has a pool of 57,50,000 equity-settled options; half vest over three years from grant date, the remainder over three years starting from the first anniversary, and vested options must be exercised within five years.

structure.title: 20. Risk Management
structure.summary: The text details the Bank's Enterprise-wide Risk Management framework, emphasizing independent risk oversight and alignment with business strategy. It covers Credit Risk Management, including policies, rating models, portfolio analysis, exposure limits, stress testing, early warning systems, and digital underwriting. Market Risk Management is described with VaR, sensitivity limits, and daily valuation. Asset-Liability Management includes liquidity risk monitoring, interest rate risk, stress testing, contingency funding, and IRRBB. Operational Risk Management covers policies, EGRC system modules, stress testing, and the Basic Indicator Approach. Systems Risk addresses IT security, ISO certification, cyber resilience, disaster recovery, and vulnerability management. Business Continuity Management outlines policy, impact analysis, recovery plans, and testing.

structure.title: 21. Priority Sector Lending (PSL)
structure.summary: The text outlines RBI's Priority Sector Lending (PSL) guidelines requiring banks to allocate 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit to sectors like agriculture, MSMEs, housing, education, social infrastructure, renewable energy, export credit, and weaker sections. It details the Bank's strategic alignment of business verticals, tailored product development, and digital initiatives for MSMEs including scorecard-based credit assessment and GST integration. It mentions 126 specialized MSME branches as of March 31, 2025. The text covers the Bank's allocation to funds like RIDF due to PSL shortfalls, with deposits of ₹5,604.67 crore, and its use of PSLCs, purchasing ₹51,431 crore and selling ₹14,882 crore in FY2025. It concludes that the Bank is fulfilling PSL commitments through innovation, digital enablement, dedicated branches, and regulatory instruments.

structure.title: 22. Marketing and Communications
structure.summary: IndusInd Bank's FY2025 marketing and communications focused on enhancing brand visibility, customer engagement, and loyalty through campaigns like the 30 Years celebration, ICC T20 World Cup 2024 global partnership (#GoLimitless), and INDIE brand initiatives. Product launches included Indus Care/Grande Care savings accounts, Indus One Business Account, PIONEER Private banking and credit card, and co-branded eLITE RuPay Credit Card. The Consumer Finance Division used WhatsApp creatives and contests for vehicle and home loans. Other initiatives covered cyber fraud awareness (Jaankaar Bano, Jagruk Raho), Loan Utsav, and the Great Indian Loan Festival. Employee engagement programs, zonal branch activities, metro/airport OOH branding, sports partnerships (Paralympic Games, blind cricket), CSR communications, and recognition awards were also detailed.

structure.title: 23. IndusInd for Sports

structure.title: 24. Corporate Social Responsibility
structure.summary: IndusInd Bank's CSR initiative, SATTVAM, focuses on economic inclusion, social equity, and environmental sustainability, aligned with national priorities and UN SDGs. Its Holistic Rural Development Flagship Program targets five aspirational districts using six strategic pillars: long-term commitment, collaboration, convergence, community ownership, technology and innovation, and monitoring and evaluation. Other CSR initiatives cover remedial education, scholarships, farmer livelihoods, inclusive sports, armed forces welfare, veteran business incubation, and cancer patient support. Awards in 2024-2025 recognize water conservation, inclusive sports, rural development, and climate-resilient initiatives.

nodes.title: Sport India Awards 2024
key_items: Project | Thematic Area: Overall CSR Portfolio
nodes.summary: The text highlights four CSR awards received in 2024. The Sport India Award recognized inclusive sports initiatives supporting women, PWDs, and marginalized groups, impacting 1,010+ athletes. The CSR Journal Excellence Award honored a comprehensive development program across seven villages in Jawahar, Maharashtra, benefiting over 8,000 individuals through water infrastructure, sustainable farming, and livelihood enhancement. The IIT Madras CSR Award recognized a technology-driven Landscape Learning model and rainfall assessment system implemented in three aspirational districts to inform climate-responsive policy. The Times Now Champions of CSR Award acknowledged overall CSR efforts in sustainable development, community engagement, and responsible business practices.

nodes.title: CII Water Awards 2024
nodes.summary: The text announces three awards received by IndusInd Bank Limited for water and environmental initiatives. The CII Water Awards 2024 recognized the Holistic Rural Development Program in Virudhunagar, Tamil Nadu, for rejuvenating an ancient natural tank system to improve water storage and conservation. The FICCI Water Awards 2024 honored the Springshed Conservation and Management project in South Odisha for enhancing water accessibility and agricultural productivity, benefiting over 7,000 families across 82 villages with irrigated farmland, agroforestry, water conservation, and drinking water filters. The ICC Social Impact Awards 2025 recognized the Usharmukti Program in West Bengal, a collaborative effort to revitalize 15,000 hectares of barren land across six districts, enhancing water security and livelihoods for 70,000 households through MGNREGA and watershed development.

structure.title: 25. Sustainability

nodes.title: 25. Sustainability (intro)
nodes.summary: The text outlines IndusInd Bank's sustainability strategy, governance, and ESG products. Governance is structured via a Board CSR & Sustainability Committee, Sustainability Council, team, and BU contacts, each with defined roles. nodes.title: Sustainability

structure.title: 6. Foreign Exchange and Derivative Contracts
structure.summary: The text details IndusInd Bank's accounting policies for foreign exchange and derivative contracts. It covers revaluation of trading forward exchange contracts using FEDAI rates or market/swap curves with gains/losses recognized on present value basis. Swap costs on foreign currency swaps are amortized over the contract life. Derivative contracts are designated as hedging or trading: hedging contracts (FRAs, interest rate swaps, currency swaps) account net interest on accrual basis, with mark-to-market adjustments for designated assets/liabilities and termination gains/losses per RBI guidelines. Trading contracts (forwards, swaps, FRAs, futures, options, swaptions) are fair-valued with gains/losses in profit and loss. Currency option premiums are accounted when due. Fair value is determined via market quotes or valuation models considering market factors. RBI guidelines require reversing overdue receivables (>90 days) and mark-to-market gains on derivative contracts with the same counterparties through profit and loss.
